The PDF on Moodle (Intro_AI.pdf) was created on 5 Oct 2025, i.e. it is last year's deck. The lecture on 12 Oct 2026 may use an updated version; if new slides appear on Moodle, diff them against this one.

The big picture

The lecture answers "what is AI, where did it come from, and where is it in your degree?". Definitions of AI fall into a 2 × 2 grid: systems that think or act, measured against humans or against an ideal of rationality. The "humanly" side is the old dream of strong AI (a machine with a mind; tested by Turing's test, attacked by Searle's Chinese room); the "rationally" side is weak AI: systems that do a specific task well, which is what actually works today. The history is a series of booms and busts: expert systems in the 1980s, then game-playing (Deep Blue, AlphaGo), question answering (Watson) and large language models. Technically, weak AI has two traditions: symbolic (knowledge written as logic by experts, exact reasoning) and subsymbolic (knowledge learned from data as numbers, probabilistic), with deep learning the dominant subsymbolic method. Their combination, hybrid AI, is one route towards broad AI that spans several tasks. The rest of the deck maps all this onto the courses of the programme and the AI research at the faculty.

Outlook

  • What is AI?
  • A (very) short history of AI
  • Weak AI and beyond
  • AI topics in the programme
  • TEWI: an AI perspective

What is AI?

Systems thinking like humans

  • "The exciting new effort to make computers think … machines with minds, in the full and literal sense." (Haugland, 1985)
  • "[The automation of] activities that we associate with human thinking, activities such as decision making, problem solving, learning." (Bellman, 1978)

Systems acting like humans

  • "The art of creating machines that perform functions that require intelligence when performed by people." (Kurzweil, 1990)
  • "The study of how to make computers do the things at which, at the moment, people are better." (Rich and Knight, 1991)

Systems thinking rationally

  • "The study of mental faculties through the use of computational models." (Charniak and McDermott, 1985)
  • "The study of the computations that make it possible to perceive, reason, and act." (Winston, 1992)

Systems acting rationally

  • "Computational Intelligence is the study of the design of intelligent agents." (Poole et al., 1998)
  • "AI … is concerned with intelligent behaviour in artifacts." (Nilsson, 1998)
Intuition — the 2 × 2 grid

The eight quotes sort along two questions: does the definition care about thinking (the process inside) or acting (the behaviour outside)? And is the yardstick human performance or rationality (doing the right thing given the goal)?

humanlyrationally
thinkingcognitive modelling: how do people think?laws of thought: logic
actingTuring test: behave like a personrational agents: act to best achieve a goal

This grid is the opening of Russell & Norvig's textbook Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, which the "acting rationally" item cites. Engineering AI today lives almost entirely in the bottom-right cell.

Types of AI

  • The view of "strong AI":

    • thinking humanly: cognitive science (information-processing psychology);
    • acting humanly: Turing Test (A. Turing, 1950) — heavily criticised: Chinese room (J. Searle, 1980).

  • More "weak AI":

    • thinking rationally: laws of thought (G. Boole, 1854), logic;
    • acting rationally: design agents that "do the right thing" (behave well; S. Russell & P. Norvig, 1995).

Ernie Davies (2014): "There are a number of cognitive tasks people do easily — often, indeed, with no conscious thought at all — but that are hard to do for computers. Archetypical examples are vision, natural language understanding, and 'real world reasoning'."

Unclear (slides 4, 6)

Two author names are misspelled on the slides: "Haugland" is John Haugeland, and "Ernie Davies" is Ernest (Ernie) Davis, NYU. The quotes themselves are as printed.

What is the Turing test, and what does the Chinese room argue against it?

Turing test (1950): a human judge chats in text with a hidden partner. If the judge can't reliably tell whether the partner is a machine or a person, the machine "passes": acting humanly is taken as the test of intelligence. Chinese room (Searle, 1980): a person who knows no Chinese sits in a room with a rule book. Chinese questions come in; by matching symbols against the rules, the person sends out perfect Chinese answers. From outside, the room passes the test, yet nobody inside understands a word. Searle's point: manipulating symbols by rules (which is all a program does) is not the same as understanding. So passing the Turing test would show acting humanly, not thinking humanly, and doesn't settle strong AI.

Overview diagram (slide 7):

  • Artificial Intelligence — creation of intelligent systems and machines that can perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence. Two kinds:

    • Artificial General Intelligence — AI capable of understanding, learning, and applying knowledge flexibly across different domains, matching or exceeding human-level cognitive abilities.
    • Weak AI Methods — AI systems specialised in performing a specific task or set of tasks, but unable to generalise beyond their programmed domain.
Common mistake — "weak AI" means "bad AI"

"Weak" refers to the scope of the claim, not the quality. A weak-AI chess engine beats every human; a weak-AI image classifier can exceed human accuracy (see the AI Index chart below). It's "weak" because it can do only its task and makes no claim to a mind. Everything in this degree, including large language models, is weak AI in this sense.

A (very) short history of AI

The roaring 1980s of AI

  • Successful domain-specific systems (MYCIN, XCON, …) sparked huge interest.
  • Expert systems (XPS) everywhere.
  • Ambitious projects around the globe (5th Generation, CYC, ECRC, MCC, …).
  • Thousands of people at AI conferences.
  • Expectations were flying high …

Slide 10 repeats the title with only a picture of a frozen, snowed-in city.

Context — the frozen picture

The image stands for the AI winter that followed: the expert-system boom ended in the late 1980s, when the systems proved expensive to build and maintain and brittle outside their narrow domain; funding and interest collapsed. A similar winter had followed the over-optimism of the 1960s (see the perceptron below). The pattern "hype → disappointment → winter" is why the deck lists what's missing so carefully.

Deep Blue (1997)

  • IBM's Deep Blue beats World Champion Garry Kasparov.
  • A milestone in man vs. machine gaming.
  • Conventional game search techniques, massive hardware.

IBM Watson (2011)

  • IBM's DeepQA project: answer questions in natural language.
  • Massive text databases and heuristic search (run many algorithms).
  • Wins against Jeopardy champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter.
  • Commercial exploitation: consultancy aid, e.g. medical; legal (Ross Intelligence); autonomous vehicles (Olli bus).

AlphaGo (2015/2016)

  • Deep learning (Google's DeepMind company):

    • applied first to Atari games;
    • combines neural networks with search techniques (Monte Carlo Tree Search).
  • Go is considered notoriously hard (PSPACE-complete).
  • Other games before (checkers 2007, poker not yet fully).
  • Nominated for the Marvin Minsky Medal.
Why was Go so much harder for computers than chess?

Deep Blue's method, searching the game tree move by move, depends on how many options there are per move and how well a position can be scored. Chess has about 35 legal moves per position; Go about 250, and games are much longer, so the tree is astronomically larger. And there was no good hand-written formula to score a Go position. AlphaGo's step was to learn the scoring and the promising moves with neural networks from games, and use them to guide the search (Monte Carlo Tree Search) to the few branches worth exploring: subsymbolic learning combined with classic search.

Large language models

  • Natural language understanding:

    • encapsulate vast amounts of world knowledge across domains;
    • streamline language-based tasks;
    • context-aware suggestions and insights from unstructured data;
    • easily fine-tuned or prompted for specific domains and applications.
  • Lower barriers to advanced AI capabilities.
  • Benefit from ongoing model updates and transfer learning.

Figure on the slide: a timeline "Evolution of Large Language Models".

Intuition — the four milestones as four methods

Deep Blue = search with hand-written evaluation (symbolic). Watson = many algorithms over huge text databases, choosing among candidate answers. AlphaGo = search guided by learned neural networks. LLMs = one huge neural network trained on text, used for many tasks by prompting. The trend over 25 years: less hand-written knowledge, more learned from data.

Weak AI and beyond

Symbolic and subsymbolic AI

SymbolicSubsymbolic
Knowledge is represented as symbols and logical expressions: img-id01 has_physical_failure FusedWire, FusedWire SubClassOf PhysicalFailureRepresentations use mathematical expressions (various functions): the model w_0 + w_1 T + w_2 E > 0 captures knowledge as coefficients (w_0, w_1, w_2)
Deductive acquisition: domain experts specify their knowledge using formal languages, e.g. ontologiesInductive acquisition: domain knowledge is acquired from provided examples
Precise inference results using search and optimisation methodsProbabilistic methods handle uncertainty in inputs and decision procedures
w_0 + w_1 T + w_2 E > 0
Symbols
  • T — "source life" in the example (s), the horizontal axis of the plot below
  • E — "beam energy" (keV), the vertical axis
  • w_0, w_1, w_2 — the model's coefficients (weights), learned from examples; in the example w_0 = 3, w_1 = 1.5, w_2 = -2 (units such that each term is a pure number)
  • "> 0" — the decision rule: if the weighted sum is positive, predict class "positive" (implantation success), otherwise "negative"

Knowledge representation examples

Symbolic: a failure-analysis knowledge graph. Ontology classes (green: Physical, FusedWire, BondWire), knowledge-graph nodes (blue: images, reports, URLs) and database entries (purple: jobs) linked by named relations such as has_physical_failure, stored_at, SubClassOf.

Subsymbolic: "Implantation Success" — the projection of a 2D separation plane on the feature space. Model w_0 + w_1 T + w_2 E > 0, coefficients w_0 = 3, w_1 = 1.5, w_2 = -2; the red line separates the "Positive" (green) from the "Negative" (blue) region.

Unclear (slide 17)

The region labels don't match the printed model. The red line is where 3 + 1.5\,T - 2E = 0, i.e. E = 1.5 + 0.75\,T. Above the line (the green "Positive" region) E is larger, so 3 + 1.5\,T - 2E < 0: e.g. T = 2, E = 6 gives -6. By the rule "> 0 ⇒ positive" those points would be negative. Either the labels or the sign of the coefficients (or of the inequality) are swapped on the slide. The idea of the slide is unaffected: a straight line learned from data splits the plane into two classes.

Worked example — reading a linear classifier

Use the printed model 3 + 1.5\,T - 2E and the rule "> 0 ⇒ positive".

  1. Plug in a point: T = 4\,\mathrm{s}, E = 3\,\mathrm{keV} (numbers only): 3 + 1.5 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 3 = 3.
  2. Apply the rule: 3 > 0 ⇒ predicted positive.
  3. Second point: T = 2, E = 4: 3 + 3 - 8 = -2 < 0 ⇒ predicted negative.
  4. Read the weights: w_1 > 0 means longer source life pushes towards "positive"; w_2 < 0 means higher beam energy pushes towards "negative". That's all the "knowledge" the model has: three numbers, no explanation in words. Compare the knowledge graph, where every fact is a readable sentence.
Why "deductive" for symbolic and "inductive" for subsymbolic?

Deduction goes from general rules to specific conclusions: an expert writes "FusedWire is a PhysicalFailure" and "img-id01 has a FusedWire failure", and the system derives "img-id01 has a physical failure" with certainty. Induction goes from specific examples to a general rule: the classifier sees many labelled points and generalises to a line that also decides new points, with no guarantee of being right. That's why the symbolic column says "precise inference" and the subsymbolic one "probabilistic methods handle uncertainty".

Weak AI: a bird's eye view

Weak artificial intelligence: symbolic methods (reasoning, optimisation, formal languages) serve tasks such as scheduling, planning/workflows, knowledge management, data integration and query processing; subsymbolic methods (unsupervised: clustering, representation learning; supervised: classification, regression; reinforcement: model-based, model-free; with deep learning across them) serve image analysis, text processing, measurement analysis, anomaly detection and process mining. Hybrid methods sit between the two.

Machine learning

  • McCulloch & Pitts "units" (1943), perceptron networks.
  • Incapable of expressing e.g. Boolean XOR (Papert & Minsky, 1969).
  • Almost suspended research on artificial neural networks (ANNs) for long.
  • Way out: multi-layer ANNs.

Figure on the slide: a biological neuron, an artificial unit (weighted inputs → sum → activation) and a small network.

Why can't a single perceptron compute XOR?

A single perceptron outputs 1 exactly when w_0 + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 > 0, so it splits the plane with one straight line, exactly like the classifier above. XOR is 1 for the inputs (1, 0) and (0, 1) and 0 for (0, 0) and (1, 1): the two 1-points sit on opposite corners of a square, the two 0-points on the other diagonal. No single line puts both 1-corners on one side and both 0-corners on the other. Two layers fix it: one unit computes OR, another AND, and the output combines "OR and not AND" (= XOR). That's the "way out: multi-layer ANNs".

Connection

XOR (exclusive or, \oplus) is the connective from the board notes of 1 Elements of Logic: true when exactly one input is true. And a perceptron is the same kind of model you'll meet as "neural network" in 10 Introduction to AI (Introduction to Robotics).

Deep learning

  • Deep learning: ANNs with multiple/many layers.
  • Feature extraction and learning, (un)supervised.
  • Increasing in the last decade.
  • Crux: lots of data.
  • Push for hardware (GPUs, designated chips).
  • "Data-driven" vs "model-driven" processing.

Figure on the slide: a deep neural network with input, hidden and output layers, and the features learned by successive layers (edges → combinations of edges → object parts).

AI performance benchmarks

Select AI Index technical performance benchmarks vs. human performance (AI Index 2025): performance relative to the human baseline (100 %) from 2012 to 2024 — image classification, visual reasoning, reading comprehension, English language understanding, multitask language understanding, competition-level mathematics, PhD-level science questions, multimodal reasoning. Most curves reach or pass the human baseline, the newer and harder benchmarks within one to three years.

What's missing?

  • From a cognitive perspective, a lot:

    • understanding of the mind: "brains cause minds" (J. Searle) sounds utterly simple, but how?
    • Human Brain Project (FET flagship programme): can we make an AI by simulation?
    • abstraction and deeper real-world reasoning;
    • common sense and natural language understanding.

  • From a technological perspective, too:

    • scalability, efficiency, and robustness;
    • validation and verifiability.

  • And from social and philosophical perspectives:

    • emotions;
    • ethical aspects.
Connection

The social and ethical side is the whole topic of the course Responsible Robotics and AI (this semester); validation and verifiability come back in Software Engineering and in the robotics safety topics of 8 Introduction to Human-Robot Interaction.

Lifting weak AI methods to a new level

  • Modern AI methods (weak AI) surpass human performance on a variety of tasks.
  • They fail to reach experts' performance on tasks requiring multiple competencies.
  • Broad AI methods are intended to close the gap between weak AI and AGI.
  • Hybrid AI is a subset of broad AI that can efficiently be used in industry.

Abilities of AI systems (cf. Chollet, 2019). Weak AI: AI with task-specific abilities (computer vision, natural language processing, knowledge representation & reasoning, optimisation & constraint satisfaction). Broad AI: AI abilities spanning several tasks (knowledge transfer and interaction, adaptability and robustness, abstraction and advanced reasoning, data and computational efficiency). Artificial general intelligence (AGI): human-level abilities in broad domains.

Intuition — what "hybrid" buys you

Each tradition is strong where the other is weak. Learned models handle messy perception (images, speech) but are hard to verify and need lots of data; symbolic systems are exact, explainable and need no data, but someone has to write the knowledge and they break on unforeseen input. A hybrid system lets a neural network recognise what is in the image and a symbolic layer reason about what follows (e.g. "a fused wire is a physical failure, so route the part to physical analysis"). That's why the bird's-eye diagram puts hybrid methods in the middle.

Arrows point from a course to the courses that build on it.

Connection

Your two semester-1 courses at the bottom of the map are Analysis 1 and Programming 1: everything in the AI branch rests on them. Machine Learning at the top needs both the statistics chain (Stochastics → Statistical Learning) and the AI chain.

Technical faculty: an AI perspective

(Slides by Gerhard Friedrich.)

Faculty: 9 departments · 30 research groups · 1 interdisciplinary research centre · 180 scientific staff · 1,200 students.

Structure of the presentation:

Univ.-Profs: 5 · Assoc.-Profs: 6 · Researchers: 22.

Prof. D. Jannach (Information Systems)

  • Research on recommender systems.
  • Application of machine learning methods — both data-based analytical and impact-oriented research, partly in the context of industry collaborations.
  • Research on automated error search in spreadsheets — use of both machine learning methods and symbolic methods, e.g. model-based diagnosis.
  • Research in e-commerce — e.g. dynamic pricing and customer lifetime value estimation with machine learning methods.

Prof. M. Gebser (Production Systems)

  • Large-scale wafer fabs: 1,000 production machines, 10,000 production routes, 10,000 operations per day.
  • Putting AI in the loop: 1. digital modelling & simulation; 2. offline planning & scheduling; 3. online control & dispatching; 4. empirical analysis & validation.
  • ⇒ Higher utilisation and lower tardiness.

Prof. W. Faber (Semantic Systems) — solving complex problems by formal specifications, e.g. analysis and identification of safety-critical elements.

  • Logic-based artificial intelligence, declarative programming, knowledge representation, reasoning, semantics of formal languages, planning, action reversibility, theoretical foundations.

Prof. G. Friedrich (Intelligent Systems and Business Informatics) — problem solving for "large" problem instances.

  • Knowledge representation and reasoning: configuration, planning, scheduling, model-based diagnosis, knowledge-based recommender systems.
  • Machine/deep learning for knowledge acquisition and maintenance.
  • Reinforcement learning for problem-solving.
  • Explainable AI.

Prof. J. Eder (Information and Communication Systems; Informatics Systems)

  • Temporal representation & reasoning: representation of temporal requirements; checking correctness as dynamic controllability; temporal constraints in business processes; STNUO: Simple Temporal Networks with Uncertainty and Observations.

Prof. C. Timmerer (Multimedia Communication; Information Technology) — applications of AI in video coding & streaming within the CD lab ATHENA in collaboration with Bitmovin (https://athena.itec.aau.at/).

  • Video coding: fast multi-rate encoding with machine learning (convolutional neural networks, CNNs); LiDeR: lightweight video super-resolution for mobile devices (deep neural networks, DNNs); blind visual quality assessment using vision transformers; video complexity analysis (VCA) and optimisations for per-title encoding (linear regression and random forest models).
  • Video streaming: DeepStream, video streaming enhancements using compressed DNNs; ECAS-ML, edge-assisted adaptive bitrate switching (LSTM); quality optimisation of live streaming services over HTTP with reinforcement learning (RL).

Assoc.Prof. K. Schöffmann (Multimedia Information Systems; Information Technology)

  • Medical video analysis with neural networks: tool and anatomy detection, classification and segmentation with CNNs and region-based CNNs (R-CNNs); action and event recognition with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and vision transformers.
  • Image and video retrieval with neural networks: content classification with CNNs, 3D-CNNs and vision transformers; content similarity search with CNNs and vision transformers.

Prof. M. Szölgyenyi (Stochastics; Statistics)

  • Machine learning algorithms as numerical solvers for stochastic differential equations.
  • Machine learning algorithms for solving stochastic optimal control problems.

Other study programmes dealing with AI

  • Bachelor Angewandte Informatik (in German/partly English) — elective: Artificial Intelligence and Natural Language Processing.
  • Master Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity (in English).
  • Master Informatics (in English) — electives: Artificial Intelligence; Multimedia Systems.
